claim: Over 100 years of studies in Drosophila melanogaster and related species have facilitated key discoveries in genetics, genomics, and evolution.
source: Over 100 years of studies in Drosophila melanogaster and related species in the genus Drosophila have facilitated key discoveries in genetics, genomics, and evolution.
evidence: This is a general statement about the historical importance of Drosophila research, drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: High-quality genome assemblies exist for several species in the Drosophila genus but only encompass a small fraction of the genus.
source: While high-quality genome assemblies exist for several species in this group, they only encompass a small fraction of the genus.
evidence: This statement is supported by knowledge of existing genomic resources and the diversity of the genus.

claim: This study utilized Oxford Nanopore sequencing to build genome assemblies for 101 lines of 93 drosophilid species.
source: Here, we utilize Oxford Nanopore sequencing to build an open community resource of genome assemblies for 101 lines of 93 drosophilid species encompassing 14 species groups and 35 sub-groups.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's methodology and scope.

claim: The genome assemblies encompass 14 species groups and 35 sub-groups.
source: Here, we utilize Oxford Nanopore sequencing to build an open community resource of genome assemblies for 101 lines of 93 drosophilid species encompassing 14 species groups and 35 sub-groups.
evidence: This describes the taxonomic diversity of the samples.

claim: The genomes have an average contig N50 of 10.5 Mb.
source: The genomes are highly contiguous and complete, with an average contig N50 of 10.5 Mb and greater than 97% BUSCO completeness in 97/101 assemblies.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of assembly contiguity derived from the data.

claim: 97 out of 101 assemblies have greater than 97% BUSCO completeness.
source: The genomes are highly contiguous and complete, with an average contig N50 of 10.5 Mb and greater than 97% BUSCO completeness in 97/101 assemblies.
evidence: This is a measure of assembly completeness based on BUSCO analysis.

claim: Nanopore-based assemblies are highly accurate in coding regions, particularly with respect to coding insertions and deletions.
source: We show that Nanopore-based assemblies are highly accurate in coding regions, particularly with respect to coding insertions and deletions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the reference-based quality assessment presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cost of a highly contiguous and complete Drosophila assembly based on long-read sequencing is about $1,000 US dollars.
source: Long reads have proved to be a way to quickly generate affordable yet high-quality genomes, in fact the cost of a highly contiguous and complete Drosophila assembly based on long-read sequencing was recently estimated to be about $1,000 US dollars (Miller et al., 2018; Solares et al., 2018), orders of magnitude less than the first D. melanogaster genome.
evidence: This cost estimate is cited from previous publications.

claim: About two Drosophila lines can be sequenced to at least 30× depth of coverage per ONT r9.4.1 (rev D) flow cell at an approximate cost of 350 US dollars per line under ideal conditions.
source: We show that under ideal conditions, about two Drosophila lines (assuming an average 180 Mb genome) can be sequenced to at least 30× depth of coverage per ONT r9.4.1 (rev D) flow cell, at an approximate cost of 350 US dollars per line.
evidence: This is a practical estimate based on the sequencing performed in this study.

claim: D. melanogaster was the second metazoan organism to undergo whole-genome sequencing after C. elegans.
source: As a premier model organism for genetic and biological research since the foundational work of Morgan and colleagues, D. melanogaster was, after C. elegans, the second metazoan organism to undergo whole-genome sequencing (Adams et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a historical fact cited from the literature.

claim: The completion of the D. melanogaster genome proved the viability of shotgun sequencing approaches.
source: At that time, the completion of the D. melanogaster genome proved the viability of shotgun sequencing approaches and paved the way for larger, more complicated genomes (Hales et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a cited historical claim about the impact of the D. melanogaster genome project.

claim: There are representative genome assemblies available on NCBI databases for about 75 different drosophilid species (excluding genomes from this study).
source: Excluding genomes from this study, there are representative genome assemblies available on NCBI databases (GenBank and RefSeq) for about 75 different drosophilid species (Hotaling et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a cited count of existing genomic resources.

claim: About a third of the drosophilid genomes on NCBI are provided as chromosome-level scaffolds.
source: About a third of these genomes are provided as chromosome-level scaffolds.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the cited survey of NCBI resources.

claim: The family Drosophilidae includes over 1600 described species and possibly thousands of other undescribed species.
source: Yet even with the intense scientific interest and effort thus far, only a small portion of the remarkably diverse drosophilids, a family which includes over 1600 described and possibly thousands of other undescribed species (O'Grady and DeSalle, 2018), is available for genomic study today.
evidence: This is a cited estimate of drosophilid diversity.

claim: Most (99 of 101) of the genome assemblies are from 14 species groups in subgenera Drosophila and Sophophora of the subfamily Drosophilinae.
source: Most (99 of 101) of the genome assemblies presented here are from 14 species groups in subgenera Drosophila and Sophophora of the subfamily Drosophilinae (Toda, 2020).
evidence: This describes the taxonomic composition of the dataset.

claim: One species each of the genera Leucophenga and Chymomyza from subfamily Steganinae have been sequenced.
source: One species of each of the genera Leucophenga and Chymomyza, both contained in less-studied sister subfamily Steganinae, have also been sequenced.
evidence: This describes additional taxa included in the study.

claim: The sequenced species originate from mainland and island locations in North America, Europe, Africa, and Asia.
source: The sequenced species originate from mainland and island locations in North America, Europe, Africa, and Asia; are distributed from northern (e.g. D. tristis, D.littoralis) to equatorial (e.g. D. bocqueti) latitudes; represent two independent transitions to leaf-mining herbivory (Scaptomyza and Lordiphosa); and for some species, like the pest Zaprionus indianus, represent reproductively isolated populations taken from throughout the range.
evidence: This describes the geographic diversity of the samples.

claim: The sequenced species are distributed from northern to equatorial latitudes.
source: The sequenced species originate from mainland and island locations in North America, Europe, Africa, and Asia; are distributed from northern (e.g. D. tristis, D.littoralis) to equatorial (e.g. D. bocqueti) latitudes; represent two independent transitions to leaf-mining herbivory (Scaptomyza and Lordiphosa); and for some species, like the pest Zaprionus indianus, represent reproductively isolated populations taken from throughout the range.
evidence: This describes the latitudinal diversity of the samples.

claim: Scaptomyza and Lordiphosa represent two independent transitions to leaf-mining herbivory.
source: The sequenced species originate from mainland and island locations in North America, Europe, Africa, and Asia; are distributed from northern (e.g. D. tristis, D.littoralis) to equatorial (e.g. D. bocqueti) latitudes; represent two independent transitions to leaf-mining herbivory (Scaptomyza and Lordiphosa); and for some species, like the pest Zaprionus indianus, represent reproductively isolated populations taken from throughout the range.
evidence: This is a statement about the ecological diversity and evolutionary history of the sampled taxa.

claim: Under optimal conditions, Nanopore sequencing runs should net 12–15 Gb of data per R9.4.1 flow cell with a read N50 greater than 20 kb.
source: Under optimal conditions and with enough starting material (at least 2,000 ng of very high molecular weight DNA) to prepare at least three library loads (~1200–500 ng total prepared library, 350–500 ng per load), along with regular DNAse flushes to maintain yields, Nanopore sequencing runs following the supplied protocol should net 12–15 Gb of data per R9.4.1 flow cell with a read N50 greater than 20 kb, and about 30% of data in reads longer than 50 kb.
evidence: This is a practical guideline based on the sequencing performed in this study.

claim: About 30% of Nanopore sequencing data should be in reads longer than 50 kb under optimal conditions.
source: Under optimal conditions and with enough starting material (at least 2,000 ng of very high molecular weight DNA) to prepare at least three library loads (~1200–500 ng total prepared library, 350–500 ng per load), along with regular DNAse flushes to maintain yields, Nanopore sequencing runs following the supplied protocol should net 12–15 Gb of data per R9.4.1 flow cell with a read N50 greater than 20 kb, and about 30% of data in reads longer than 50 kb.
evidence: This is a practical guideline based on the sequencing performed in this study.

claim: 94 of 101 assemblies contain over 98% of the assembly in contigs larger than 10 kb.
source: Of 101 total assemblies, 94 contain over 98% of the assembly in contigs larger than 10 kb, and both contig N50s and NG50s exceed 1 Mb for these genomes (Figure 1A, Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of assembly contiguity.

claim: Contig N50s and NG50s exceed 1 Mb for 94 genomes.
source: Of 101 total assemblies, 94 contain over 98% of the assembly in contigs larger than 10 kb, and both contig N50s and NG50s exceed 1 Mb for these genomes (Figure 1A, Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of assembly contiguity.

claim: Assembly sizes were highly correlated with estimated genome sizes.
source: Assembly sizes were highly correlated with estimated genome sizes (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Of the 76 representative drosophilid genomes previously available on NCBI, only 25 have an N50 greater than 1 Mb.
source: For comparison, of the 76 representative drosophilid genomes that were previously available on NCBI (Hotaling et al., 2021), only 25 have an N50 greater than 1 Mb (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparison to existing resources based on cited data.

claim: BUSCO completeness is in the range of 97–99+% for all but the three most fragmented genomes.
source: High contiguity resulted in benchmarking universal single-copy ortholog (BUSCO) completeness (Seppey et al., 2019; Simão et al., 2015) in the range of 97–99+% for all but the three most fragmented genomes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a measure of assembly completeness based on BUSCO analysis.

claim: Estimated SNP heterozygosity ranged from 0.00035% to 1.1% from long reads and 0.0015% to 2.1% from short reads.
source: Estimated SNP heterozygosity, the number of heterozygous SNPs divided by the number of callable sites, ranged from 0.00035% to 1.1% from long reads and 0.0015% to 2.1% from short reads, and heterozygosity estimated from long reads was systematically lower than that from short reads, particularly when sample diversity was high (Figure 2, Figure S6).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of sample diversity derived from variant calling.

claim: Heterozygosity estimated from long reads was systematically lower than that from short reads, particularly when sample diversity was high.
source: Estimated SNP heterozygosity, the number of heterozygous SNPs divided by the number of callable sites, ranged from 0.00035% to 1.1% from long reads and 0.0015% to 2.1% from short reads, and heterozygosity estimated from long reads was systematically lower than that from short reads, particularly when sample diversity was high (Figure 2, Figure S6).
evidence: This is an observation from the variant calling analysis.

claim: No significant relationship was observed between estimated heterozygosity and assembly contiguity.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe a significant relationship (p=0.30) between estimated heterozygosity and assembly contiguity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis.

claim: The number of heterozygous non-reference variants almost always exceeded the number of homozygous variants.
source: The number of heterozygous non-reference variants almost always exceeded the number of homozygous variants (Supplementary file 3), as would be expected from residual diversity in the sequenced lines.
evidence: This is an observation from the variant calling analysis.

claim: Phred-scaled consensus quality (QV) estimated from short reads ranged from QV17 to QV45.
source: As expected from the patterns of heterozygosity estimated from long and short reads, there was a large amount of variability in quality scores. Estimates from short reads ranged from QV17 to QV45 and from long reads were slightly higher, from QV19 to QV52 (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of sequence quality.

claim: Phred-scaled consensus quality (QV) estimated from long reads ranged from QV19 to QV52.
source: As expected from the patterns of heterozygosity estimated from long and short reads, there was a large amount of variability in quality scores. Estimates from short reads ranged from QV17 to QV45 and from long reads were slightly higher, from QV19 to QV52 (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of sequence quality.

claim: Merqury-estimated quality scores ranged from QV16 to QV40.
source: Estimated quality scores ranged from QV16 to QV40, and once again, samples for which reads from a different strain or a genetically diverse sample (i.e. wild samples or recent isolates) were used had the lowest estimated QV.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of sequence quality using a reference-free method.

claim: Merqury-estimated QV was on average higher than consensus quality estimated by variant calling methods.
source: Merqury-estimated QV was on average higher than consensus quality estimated by the variant calling methods, but the relative ranking of QV estimates remained largely consistent with QV based on short-read (Spearman's ρ=0.642, p<2.2e-16) and long-read (Spearman's ρ=0.684, p<2.2e-16) variant calls.
evidence: This is a comparison of different quality estimation methods.

claim: Sequence accuracy varied greatly within each genome assembly.
source: As expected, we found that sequence accuracy varied greatly within each genome assembly (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the reference-based quality assessment.

claim: Mean genome-wide QV ranged from QV15 to QV24 in reference-based assessments.
source: Mean genome-wide QV ranged from QV15 to QV24 while median QV across the 100 kb windows ranged from QV14 to QV36.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure from the reference-based quality assessment.

claim: Median QV across 100 kb windows ranged from QV14 to QV36 in reference-based assessments.
source: Mean genome-wide QV ranged from QV15 to QV24 while median QV across the 100 kb windows ranged from QV14 to QV36.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure from the reference-based quality assessment.

claim: When looking only at coding sequences, mean QV ranged from QV23 to QV29.
source: When looking only at coding sequences, mean QV ranged from QV23 to QV29, while the median window accuracy, with the exceptions of D. grimshawi (QV25) and D. rhopaloa (QV30), indicated complete identity (>QV50) between assembly and reference.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of coding sequence accuracy.

claim: The median window accuracy for coding sequences indicated complete identity (>QV50) between assembly and reference, with exceptions of D. grimshawi (QV25) and D. rhopaloa (QV30).
source: When looking only at coding sequences, mean QV ranged from QV23 to QV29, while the median window accuracy, with the exceptions of D. grimshawi (QV25) and D. rhopaloa (QV30), indicated complete identity (>QV50) between assembly and reference.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of coding sequence accuracy.

claim: Median QV across windows always exceeded mean QV, often by more than QV10.
source: However, regardless of the genomic element type, median QV across the windows always exceeded mean QV, often by more than QV10, or an order of magnitude difference in the error rate.
evidence: This is an observation about the distribution of errors in the assemblies.

claim: Differences between Nanopore and reference assemblies were clustered heavily into a few genomic regions.
source: In other words, differences between Nanopore and reference assemblies were clustered heavily into a few genomic regions, and most coding sequences were very accurate despite the seemingly high mean error rate (Figure 3B, Figure 3C, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an inference from the distribution of quality scores.

claim: Most coding sequences were very accurate despite the seemingly high mean error rate.
source: In other words, differences between Nanopore and reference assemblies were clustered heavily into a few genomic regions, and most coding sequences were very accurate despite the seemingly high mean error rate (Figure 3B, Figure 3C, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an inference from the distribution of quality scores.

claim: Across 22,209,264 bp of D. melanogaster genome aligned to reference coding sequences, the assembly contained 15 insertions and 17 deletions in 21 out of 13,913 (0.15%) queried protein-coding genes.
source: Across the 22,209,264 bp of our D. melanogaster genome that aligned to reference coding sequences, our assembly contained 15 insertions and 17 deletions in 21 out of 13,913 (0.15%) queried protein-coding genes, with a total of 10,092 inserted and 46 deleted base pairs relative to the reference.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of coding sequence differences in D. melanogaster.

claim: All deletions in D. melanogaster coding sequences were under 50 bp.
source: All deletions (15 out of 15) were under 50 bp, 8 out of 15 insertions were under 50 bp, and the remaining 7 out of 15 insertions ranged from 120 bp to 4410 bp (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative characterization of indels in D. melanogaster.

claim: 8 out of 15 insertions in D. melanogaster coding sequences were under 50 bp, and the remaining 7 ranged from 120 bp to 4410 bp.
source: All deletions (15 out of 15) were under 50 bp, 8 out of 15 insertions were under 50 bp, and the remaining 7 out of 15 insertions ranged from 120 bp to 4410 bp (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative characterization of indels in D. melanogaster.

claim: Large insertions account for nearly all (99.3%) of the coding sequence differences between the Nanopore assembly and the D. melanogaster reference.
source: These larger insertions account for nearly all (99.3%) of the coding sequence differences between our genome and the reference.
evidence: This is a quantitative characterization of the impact of large insertions.

claim: Manual curation revealed that coding indels could be straightforwardly explained by regions of poor short read mapping and the presence of a duplicate contig in the assembly.
source: This manual curation process revealed that the coding indels, in addition to being exceedingly rare, could be straightforwardly explained by regions of poor short read mapping and the presence of a duplicate contig in the assembly (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the manual validation of indels.

claim: Four out of five insertions longer than 100 bp overlapped a tandem repeat in genes CR44666, Mu68Ca, and Mu68E.
source: A series of large and small indels, including four out of the five insertions longer than 100 bp, overlapped a tandem repeat in genes CR44666, Mu68Ca, and Mu68E.
evidence: This is a finding from the manual curation of D. melanogaster indels.

claim: Long reads spanning the entire region and two other long-read assemblies supported the large insertions in tandem repeat regions.
source: While short reads mapped poorly to this region, limiting our ability to determine accuracy locally, long reads spanning the entire region and the two other long-read assemblies supported the large insertions.
evidence: This is evidence supporting the accuracy of the Nanopore assembly in specific regions.

claim: Reference-based quality analyses can be heavily biased against long-read assemblies.
source: Importantly, these results suggest that reference-based quality analyses can be heavily biased against long-read assemblies and further support our caution against a naive projection of genome-wide quality score estimates onto coding regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the manual validation results.

claim: BUSCOs formed six major clusters following the D. melanogaster chromosome arm on which they are found.
source: We found that BUSCOs formed six major clusters following the D. melanogaster chromosome arm on which they are found, consistent with the expected conservation of gene content in Muller elements across drosophilids (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the synteny analysis.

claim: The clustering of BUSCOs is consistent with the expected conservation of gene content in Muller elements across drosophilids.
source: We found that BUSCOs formed six major clusters following the D. melanogaster chromosome arm on which they are found, consistent with the expected conservation of gene content in Muller elements across drosophilids (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the synteny analysis in the context of known biology.

claim: The lack of a clear order within BUSCO groups is consistent with extensive shuffling within Muller elements.
source: Furthermore, the lack of a clear order within groups is consistent with extensive shuffling within Muller elements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the synteny analysis.

claim: No correlation exists between assembly contiguity and repeat content.
source: No correlation exists between assembly contiguity and repeat content (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting long-read sequencing overcomes many of the challenges to drosophilid genome assembly posed by repetitive sequences.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the repeat analysis.

claim: Long-read sequencing overcomes many of the challenges to drosophilid genome assembly posed by repetitive sequences.
source: No correlation exists between assembly contiguity and repeat content (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting long-read sequencing overcomes many of the challenges to drosophilid genome assembly posed by repetitive sequences.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of correlation between contiguity and repeat content.

claim: A positive relationship exists between the size of repetitive sequences and non-repetitive sequences.
source: Additionally, we observe a positive relationship between the size of repetitive sequences and non-repetitive sequences, suggesting that genome size is influenced by expansions and contractions of both portions of the genome (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the phylogenetically independent contrasts analysis.

claim: Genome size is influenced by expansions and contractions of both repetitive and non-repetitive portions of the genome.
source: Additionally, we observe a positive relationship between the size of repetitive sequences and non-repetitive sequences, suggesting that genome size is influenced by expansions and contractions of both portions of the genome (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the positive relationship between repetitive and non-repetitive sequence sizes.

claim: Flye was chosen as the assembler based on superior contiguity and favorable runtimes relative to Miniasm and Canu.
source: We chose Flye (Kolmogorov et al., 2019) as our assembler based on superior contiguity and favorable runtimes relative to Miniasm (Li, 2016) and Canu (Koren et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on benchmarking.

claim: High contiguity can be achieved even with minimal (10–20×) coverage of moderately long (read N50 25 kb) Nanopore reads.
source: Interestingly, we find that high contiguity can be achieved even with minimal (10–20×) coverage of moderately long (read N50 25 kb) Nanopore reads (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the downsampling analysis.

claim: Near chromosome scale assemblies (N50>20Mb) were achievable even at 15× to 20× depth with a read N50 of ~27.5 kb.
source: Near chromosome scale assemblies (N50>20Mb) were achievable even at 15× to 20× depth with this read length distribution.
evidence: This is a finding from the downsampling analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The modified workflow increases the yield of ultra-long reads relative to the standard ligation kit protocol.
source: This modified workflow is optimized for genomic DNA extractions from 15 to 30 whole flies, increases the yield of ultra-long reads relative to the standard ligation kit protocol, increases overall sequencing throughput, and significantly reduces the cost of library preparation.
evidence: This is a claim about the benefits of the modified protocol.

claim: The modified workflow increases overall sequencing throughput.
source: This modified workflow is optimized for genomic DNA extractions from 15 to 30 whole flies, increases the yield of ultra-long reads relative to the standard ligation kit protocol, increases overall sequencing throughput, and significantly reduces the cost of library preparation.
evidence: This is a claim about the benefits of the modified protocol.

claim: The modified workflow significantly reduces the cost of library preparation.
source: This modified workflow is optimized for genomic DNA extractions from 15 to 30 whole flies, increases the yield of ultra-long reads relative to the standard ligation kit protocol, increases overall sequencing throughput, and significantly reduces the cost of library preparation.
evidence: This is a claim about the benefits of the modified protocol.

claim: The ordering of genes in drosophilid chromosomal (Muller) elements has been extensively shuffled throughout ~53 million years of evolution.
source: Although the ordering of genes in drosophilid chromosomal (Muller) elements has been extensively shuffled throughout ~53 million years of evolution (Suvorov et al., 2021), the gene content of each element remains largely conserved (Bracewell et al., 2019; Ranz et al., 2001; Sturtevant and Novitski, 1941).
evidence: This is a cited statement about drosophilid genome evolution.

claim: The gene content of each Muller element remains largely conserved.
source: Although the ordering of genes in drosophilid chromosomal (Muller) elements has been extensively shuffled throughout ~53 million years of evolution (Suvorov et al., 2021), the gene content of each element remains largely conserved (Bracewell et al., 2019; Ranz et al., 2001; Sturtevant and Novitski, 1941).
evidence: This is a cited statement about drosophilid genome evolution.

claim: Genome size was estimated with Nanopore and Illumina data separately.
source: Genome size was estimated with Nanopore and Illumina data separately (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the methodology for genome size estimation.

claim: GenomeScope was used to estimate genome size from Illumina reads using a k-mer counting approach.
source: To estimate genome size from Illumina reads, we used the k-mer counting approach implemented in GenomeScope v1.0.0 (Vurture et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the methodology for genome size estimation from short reads.

claim: Regions annotated as single-copy BUSCO genes were used to estimate genome size from long reads.
source: Since the higher error rate of Nanopore reads (5–15%) precludes the use of k-mer based reference-free approaches for genome size estimation, we instead used regions annotated as a single-copy BUSCO gene to estimate genome size.
evidence: This describes the methodology for genome size estimation from long reads.

claim: The higher error rate of Nanopore reads (5–15%) precludes the use of k-mer based reference-free approaches for genome size estimation.
source: Since the higher error rate of Nanopore reads (5–15%) precludes the use of k-mer based reference-free approaches for genome size estimation, we instead used regions annotated as a single-copy BUSCO gene to estimate genome size.
evidence: This is a rationale for the chosen methodology.

claim: Flye produced significantly more contiguous assemblies than those reported by Miller et al. 2018.
source: In addition to a much shorter (8–12 hr wall-clock time) runtime, Flye also produced significantly more contiguous assemblies than those reported by Miller et al. (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a comparison of assembly methods.

claim: Canu produced relatively contiguous assemblies but a single assembly took several days on a 92-core cloud server.
source: Canu produced relatively contiguous assemblies, but a single assembly took several days on a 92-core cloud server and even longer when a large number of extra-long (>50kb) reads were present in the data.
evidence: This is an observation about the computational requirements of Canu.

claim: Haplotig identification and removal was performed if the BUSCO duplication rate exceeded 1%.
source: If the BUSCO duplication rate exceeded 1%, haplotig identification and removal was performed, but on the draft assembly produced by Flye rather than the polished assembly.
evidence: This describes a conditional step in the assembly pipeline.

claim: Allowing Pilon to fix gaps or local misassemblies in default mode introduced large spurious indels in regions where short reads map poorly.
source: We found that allowing Pilon to fix gaps or local misassemblies in default mode introduced large spurious indels in regions where short reads map poorly such as tandem repeats.
evidence: This is an observation about the behavior of Pilon.

claim: Spurious indels introduced by Pilon were not supported by long reads or by comparison to a reference assembly.
source: These variants were not supported by long reads or by comparison to a reference assembly.
evidence: This is evidence that the indels were errors.

claim: BLAST was used to remove any contigs not associated with at least one BUSCO that were also of bacterial, protozoan, or fungal origin.
source: We used BLAST v2.10.0 (Altschul et al., 1990) to remove any contigs not associated with at least one BUSCO that were also of bacterial, protozoan, or fungal origin.
evidence: This describes the decontamination procedure.

claim: Any sequences flagged by the NCBI Contamination Screen were excluded or trimmed.
source: Finally, any sequences flagged by the NCBI Contamination Screen were excluded or trimmed.
evidence: This describes the decontamination procedure.

claim: Each draft assembly was soft repeat masked with RepeatMasker at medium sensitivity.
source: Each draft assembly was soft repeat masked with RepeatMasker v4.1.0 (Smit et al., 2013) at medium sensitivity, with both Dfam 3.1 (Hubley et al., 2016) and RepBase RepeatMasker edition (Bao et al., 2015) repeat libraries installed (options: --species Drosophila --xsmall).
evidence: This describes the repeat masking procedure.

claim: The auN statistic is the area under an Nx curve.
source: The auN statistic (Li, 2020) is the area under an Nx curve, and can be computed by multiplying the length of each contig (Li) by the proportion of the assembled genome it accounts for (Li /∑Li), then summing these values for all i contigs
evidence: This is a definition of a statistical measure.

claim: auN is always sensitive to a break in the assembly.
source: Contig N50 represents a single point on the Nx curve and may or may not be affected by assembly breaks, but auN is always sensitive to a break in the assembly.
evidence: This is a property of the auN statistic.

claim: auN is a fairer statistic for comparison between different versions of the same assembly than contig N50.
source: Therefore, auN is a fairer statistic for comparison between different versions of the same assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of auN.

claim: BUSCO v3 was used during the assembly process for all assemblies.
source: When this work was started, BUSCO v3 was the current version. Version 4 was released while the project was ongoing. For consistency, version three was used during the assembly process for all assemblies, but the completeness of all final assemblies was assessed with BUSCO v4.
evidence: This describes the versioning of BUSCO used in the study.

claim: The completeness of all final assemblies was assessed with BUSCO v4.
source: When this work was started, BUSCO v3 was the current version. Version 4 was released while the project was ongoing. For consistency, version three was used during the assembly process for all assemblies, but the completeness of all final assemblies was assessed with BUSCO v4.
evidence: This describes the versioning of BUSCO used in the study.

claim: Variants were called with PEPPER-Margin-Deepvariant for long reads and BCFtools for short reads.
source: Long and short reads (if available) were mapped separately to each finished genome and variant calling was performed with PEPPER-Margin-DeepVariant (Shafin et al., 2021) for long reads and BCFtools (Danecek et al., 2021; Li, 2011) for short reads.
evidence: This describes the variant calling methodology.

claim: Only sites with minimum read depth 10, site quality score 30, and genotype quality score 30 were kept for variant analysis.
source: Only sites with minimum read depth 10, site quality score 30, and (if applicable) genotype quality score 30 filters were kept.
evidence: This describes the quality filtering applied to variant calls.

claim: Reference-free quality score estimates were computed with Merqury following the developer's instructions.
source: Reference-free quality score estimates were computed with Merqury v1.3 (Rhie et al., 2020), following the instructions provided by the developer on the GitHub repository (https://github.com/marbl/merqury).
evidence: This describes the methodology for reference-free quality assessment.

claim: Reference-based quality score estimates were computed with ONT Pomoxis for assemblies where a well-annotated counterpart of the same species and strain was available through NCBI RefSeq.
source: Reference-based quality score estimates were computed ONT Pomoxis v0.3.7 (https://github.com/nanoporetech/pomoxis) for assemblies where a well-annotated counterpart of not only the same species but the same strain was available through the NCBI RefSeq database.
evidence: This describes the methodology for reference-based quality assessment.

claim: Pomoxis aligns each Nanopore-based assembly to the reference genome and assesses differences in 100 kb windows.
source: Then, we ran Pomoxis, which aligns each Nanopore-based assembly to the reference genome and assessed differences between the two genomes in 100 kb windows (option: -c 100000).
evidence: This describes how Pomoxis was used for quality assessment.

claim: Species relationships were inferred using complete and single-copy orthologs identified by BUSCO analysis.
source: We inferred species relationships using complete and single-copy orthologs identified by the BUSCO analysis.
evidence: This describes the methodology for phylogenetic inference.

claim: 250 out of 990 single-copy orthologs present in all assemblies were randomly selected to construct gene trees.
source: Out of 990 single-copy orthologs present in all assemblies, we randomly selected 250 to construct gene trees.
evidence: This describes the sampling for phylogenetic inference.

claim: Amino acid sequences were used instead of nucleotide sequences to achieve better alignments in the face of high-sequence divergence.
source: Amino acid sequences were used instead of nucleotide sequences to achieve better alignments in the face of high-sequence divergence (Bininda-Emonds, 2005).
evidence: This is a methodological choice with a cited rationale.

claim: Gene trees were inferred with RAxML-NG using the Le and Gascuel, 2008 amino acid substitution model.
source: Gene trees were inferred with RAxML-NG v0.9.0 (Kozlov et al., 2019), using the Le and Gascuel, 2008 amino acid substitution model (options: --msa-format FASTA --data-type AA --model LG).
evidence: This describes the methodology for gene tree inference.

claim: ASTRAL-MP was used to reconstruct the species tree from gene trees.
source: The summary method ASTRAL-MP v.5.14.7 (Yin et al., 2019) was run with default settings to reconstruct the species tree.
evidence: This describes the methodology for species tree inference.

claim: The phylogenetic reconstruction is not intended to be definitive.
source: We note that this is not intended to be a definitive phylogenetic reconstruction of species relationships; see Suvorov et al., 2021 for a time-calibrated phylogeny utilizing 158 drosophilid whole genomes.
evidence: This is a caveat about the scope of the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Phylogenetically independent contrasts were computed for the counts of bases in repetitive and non-repetitive categories.
source: Phylogenetic independent contrasts (Felsenstein, 1985) were computed for the counts of bases in both categories using the R package ape v5.4.1 (Paradis and Schliep, 2019) using the species tree described above with the root age set to 53 million years following the estimate in Suvorov et al., 2021.
evidence: This describes the methodology for analyzing repeat content and genome size.

claim: Docker and Singularity were used to manage computing containers.
source: Specifically, we used the programs Docker and Singularity to manage containers.
evidence: This describes the computational infrastructure used.

claim: A Dockerfile is a text file containing instructions to set up a Docker image.
source: A Dockerfile, a text file containing instructions to set up an image, is used to select the Linux operating system and the suite of programs to be installed within a Docker container.
evidence: This is a description of Docker functionality.
